title: Build kernels and test whether a similarity is valid
brief: Compute RBF and polynomial kernel matrices with one matrix product, confirm the kernel trick on a degree-2 polynomial, test a Gram matrix with its smallest eigenvalue, and centre a Gram matrix so kernel PCA on a linear kernel matches PCA scores.
hints: For rbf_kernel, build the squared distances as a column of squared row norms plus a row of squared row norms minus 2 * X1 @ X2.T. Use [:, None] and [None, :] so the sum broadcasts to an (n1, n2) table, then clip at zero before exp.
polynomial_kernel is one line: add coef0 to the matrix of dot products, then raise every entry to the degree. Do not power X1 itself.

For poly_features_degree2, slice the two columns of X once, then stack six columns: 1, sqrt(2) x1, sqrt(2) x2, x1^2, sqrt(2) x1 x2, x2^2. Dropping a sqrt(2) is the usual reason the kernel-trick check fails.
min_eigenvalue only needs np.linalg.eigvalsh(K)[0]. eigvalsh returns real eigenvalues in ascending order for a symmetric matrix. combination_squared_length is v @ K @ v.
is_psd has three steps: return False if K is not square, return False if np.allclose(K, K.T, atol=tol, rtol=0.0) fails, then compare the smallest eigenvalue with -tol. A zero eigenvalue is allowed.
centre_gram subtracts the row mean and the column mean, then adds the mean of every entry. Subtracting the row mean only leaves the three-point top-left entry at 1/3 instead of 5/9.
